subject: Culture
title: Social Credit Systems
description: A micro-lesson that makes Social Credit Systems usable.

hook.text: In parts of China, jaywalking lowers your social credit score, blocking you from buying train tickets.

buildup.text: China's social credit system launched in 2014 to rate trustworthiness of citizens and businesses.

discovery.text: It digitized what villages always did: track reputation. But now algorithms replace gossip networks.

twist.text: Western credit scores do the same thing—they just measure financial behavior instead of social behavior.

climax.text: Every rating app—Uber, Airbnb, Yelp—is a micro social credit system we volunteered for.

punchline.text: We all live in a rating economy now.

quiz.question: When did China's social credit system officially launch?

details.summary: China's social credit system digitizes ancient honor-shame dynamics — good behavior raises your score, bad behavior lowers it, and a low score restricts travel, loans, and social opportunities.
details.whyItMatters: Social credit fuses traditional honor-shame culture with modern technology. It raises questions about whether digital reputation systems will become the global standard for social control.
takeaways: China's social credit system tracks financial, legal, and social behavior
Low scores restrict travel, loan access, and even dating prospects
Western credit scores and online reviews operate on similar principles

faq.question: How does China's social credit system work?
faq.answer: Multiple overlapping systems — government and corporate — track financial behavior (debt repayment), legal behavior (criminal records, court compliance), and social behavior (online activity, community contributions).

faq.question: Is social credit uniquely Chinese?
faq.answer: The underlying principle is not unique. Western credit scores (FICO), Uber/Airbnb ratings, employer background checks, and social media reputation effectively function as informal social credit systems.
